summary: Defines objects for managing DS3 interfaces, higher-capacity digital telephone circuits, for use with SNMP. It was replaced by RFC 1407.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a checklist for watching a big digital phone line used for data.

questions: what are errored seconds in ds3
subtitle: A set of SNMP objects for watching the health of high-capacity DS3 digital telephone circuits.

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a common way to read the configuration and error statistics of DS3 interfaces and the CSU devices attached to them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines four groups of SNMP objects (Configuration, Interval, Current and Total) that closely follow what deployed CSUs can already report, with error counts kept in 15-minute intervals.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1233 has been obsoleted by RFC 1407 and updated by RFC 1239, so it is no longer the current DS3 definition.

today: RFC 1233 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1407 and updated by RFC 1239, so it is not the current definition of the DS3 MIB.

sections.title: Purpose and Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1233 defines MIB objects for representing DS3 physical interfaces, for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets. The abstract calls it an experimental portion of the Management Information Base (MIB), and the module is placed under experimental 15.

It builds on the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: RFC 1155 (the SMI), RFC 1156 and RFC 1213 (MIB-I and MIB-II) and RFC 1157 (SNMP). Objects are described with a subset of ASN.1, using the extended OBJECT-TYPE macro from RFC 1212. Implementors are also told to read the companion document on DS1 managed objects.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small rulebook for how to name and ask about the numbers a fast phone line keeps, using the standard network-watching tools.

sections.title: Design Goals and CSU Binding
sections.content:
The objects apply when the interface type in the Internet-standard MIB is ds3 (30). They are based on three ANSI specifications: T1.102-1987, T1.107-1988 and T1.404-1989.

The aim is the common management of CSUs, both in-chassis and external via proxy. The authors chose up front to align the MIB very closely with the objects that can generally be read from CSUs already deployed.

Each agent on a host with DS3 interfaces must assign a small positive integer to each CSU, called the CSUIndex. It is the key for tabular access, and the ds3Index column of the configuration table links each CSU to its interface in the Internet-standard MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Every little box on the line gets its own number, like a locker number, so you always know which box you are asking about.

sections.title: DS3 Error Terminology
sections.content:
Error conditions follow the ANSI T1M1.3/90 draft standard. Key definitions include:

  • Out of Frame (OOF): three or more errors in sixteen or fewer consecutive F-bits within a DS3 M-frame.
  • Loss of Signal (LOS): 175 +/- 75 contiguous pulse positions with no pulses.
  • Errored Seconds (ES): a second with one or more coding violations, one or more OOF events, or an AIS.
  • Severely Errored Seconds (SES): a second with 44 or more coding violations, or one or more OOF events, or an AIS.
  • Severely Errored Framing Seconds (SEFS): a second with one or more OOF events.
  • Unavailable Seconds (UAS): seconds in the Unavailable signal state, which starts with a Red Alarm or Yellow Alarm.

A second counted as a UAS may not also count as an ES or SES, so the counters are adjusted around the 10-second transitions. The RFC admits that successive reads of the interval SES and UAS objects can differ early in a 900-second window. It calls this an unavoidable side effect.
sections.plainLanguage: It explains what counts as a bad second on the line, from a little hiccup to a really bad one, so everyone counts the same way.

sections.title: The Four Object Groups
sections.content:
All four groups are mandatory for systems attached to a DS3 interface.

  • Configuration: ds3ConfigTable with the line type, zero coding, loopback state, send code, Yellow and Red alarm flags, and a circuit identifier of up to 255 characters. Its objects are read-only, though an agent may make them read-write, for example to place the device in a loopback state.
  • Interval: statistics for the previous 24 hours, split into 96 completed 15-minute intervals, where interval 1 is the most recent.
  • Current: the same counters for the current 15-minute interval.
  • Total: the cumulative sum for the 24-hour interval before the first valid interval in the current table.

The statistics counters are ES, SES, SEFS, UAS, CSS (controlled slip seconds), BPV (bipolar violations) and CV (coding violations). CSS applies only to SYNTRAN interfaces, so other agents may treat it as not-accessible.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four notebooks. One describes the line, one keeps a page for each quarter hour of the last day, one is for right now, and one adds up the whole day.

sections.title: Line Type, Coding and Loopback Settings
sections.content:
ds3LineType says which DS3 C-bit application is in use: other(1), ds3M23(2), ds3SYNTRAN(3), ds3CbitParity(4) or ds3ClearChannel(5). The rate of all of them is 44.736 Mbps. ds3ZeroCoding is either ds3other(1) or ds3B3ZS(2).

ds3Loopback has five values, from ds3NoLoop(1) to ds3RemoteLoopbackRemoteSide(5). Devices that cannot loop back on either interface always return no loop, and a device supporting writes should return badValue for an unsupported request. M23 and ClearChannel interfaces do not support the loopback object. ds3SendCode reports what the CSU is sending, such as a loopback request or a loopback termination request.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the switches and labels on the line: what kind of line it is and whether it is currently bouncing its own signal back as a test.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Status
sections.content:
The security section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. That matters because an agent may make the configuration objects writable, for example to set a loopback, and the RFC does not say how to protect that.

The status section marks this as an IAB standards track protocol and asks for discussion and suggestions for improvement.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not say anything about keeping bad guys out. It just leaves that question open.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: Line type, zero coding, loopback, send code, alarms and circuit identifier.

items.title: Interval
items.text: Counters for each of the 96 previous 15-minute intervals.

items.title: Total
items.text: Cumulative counters for the 24-hour interval before the first valid current interval.
